procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the High Court dated 21st May 2024, rejecting the appellant's second bail application.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a second bail application before the High Court on 2nd May 2024. The High Court rejected this application on 21st May 2024.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by filing Special Leave Petition (Criminal) Nos. 7795 and 7799 of 2024 after the High Court rejected his second bail application. The Supreme Court initially disposed of a previous petition with liberty to revive the prayer after the final complaint/charge-sheet was filed. The Supreme Court then heard the appeals on their merits and ultimately allowed them (Criminal Appeal No. 3295 of 2024 and Criminal Appeal No. 3296 of 2024).

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused's right to a fair trial includes the right to inspect documents, including those not relied upon by the prosecution.

facts: The case involved a very large volume of documents, approximately 69,000 pages.
The accused took three months to inspect these documents, which included materials the prosecution did not intend to rely on ("un-relied upon documents").
The trial court and High Court found that the accused was responsible for delaying the trial by taking this time for inspection.
law: An accused person has a fundamental right to a fair trial.
application: The Supreme Court directly linked the right to a fair trial with the right to inspect all relevant documents.
It reasoned that in order to avail the right to a fair trial, an accused person cannot be denied the opportunity to inspect documents, even those the prosecution does not plan to use.
The Court considered the huge magnitude of the documents and concluded that the time taken by the accused for inspection was reasonable and necessary.
Consequently, the Court overturned the lower courts' finding that the accused was to blame for the trial's delay, stating that this finding was not supported by the record.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that an accused's right to a fair trial includes the right to inspect all documents, including those not relied upon by the prosecution. Therefore, an accused cannot be denied this right or be faulted for taking a reasonable amount of time to conduct such an inspection.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused's right to a fair trial includes the right to inspect documents, including those not relied upon by the prosecution.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, which forms the basis of the appeal, is that the right to a fair trial includes the right to inspect all documents, even those not relied upon by the prosecution.
respondent_arguments: The Additional Solicitor General (ASG), representing the respondent, expressed apprehension that allowing the appellant access could lead to the tampering of evidence and influencing of witnesses.

cases.principle: Referred to in the context of relaxing the rigours of bail conditions to grant conditional liberty.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The rigors of a statute governing bail can be relaxed to grant conditional liberty, based on the principle that bail is the rule and jail is the exception, and that bail is not to be withheld as a punishment.
obiter: Trial courts and High Courts often attempt to play safe in matters of granting bail.
The principle that bail is a rule and refusal is an exception is frequently followed in the breach.
The non-grant of bail, even in straightforward cases, results in the Supreme Court being flooded with a huge number of bail petitions, adding to judicial pendency.
